What it means: The Boston City Council Committee on Planning held a public hearing [01:00] on Docket 1718 [01:57], which proposes amending the city zoning code to prohibit data centers citywide [01:57] [07:45]. Speakers raised concerns regarding heavy energy use [02:36], grid strain [14:47], noise pollution [14:51], and potential environmental justice burdens [07:05]. Conversely, representatives from labor organizations and academic institutions argued that computing facilities support medical care [1:00:38], scientific research [1:00:38], and local employment [1:02:03], cautioning that an outright prohibition could discourage private investment and stifle innovation [1:03:15] [1:12:54].

Who moved it: The hearing was convened by Committee on Planning Chair Sharon Durkan [01:00]. Docket 1718 was co-sponsored by Councilor Minyard Culpepper [02:07] [11:07], Councilor Louijeune [05:37], and Councilor Earle [11:07].

What to watch: Planning Department officials stated that existing zoning restricts data distribution centers to three small industrial subdistricts [15:16], while councilors and panelists discussed establishing regulatory frameworks [08:07], threshold standards [31:50], or special permits as potential alternatives to a complete ban [37:42]. The transcript does not record a committee vote or final decision on Docket 1718 during this session [2:12:18].

summary: The Boston City Council held a hearing on a proposed amendment to the Boston Zoning Code regarding the definition and regulation of data centers [02:01], [07:45]. Planning department staff and councilors discussed the potential local impacts of data center infrastructure, including energy grid demands, noise, diesel emissions, and water usage [06:52], [14:45], while balancing environmental justice considerations against the computing needs of local medical, research, and educational institutions [04:09], [07:05]. Planning officials noted that the city currently hosts no hyperscale data centers [45:23] and favored updating zoning definitions and conditional review over a total citywide ban [18:57]. Panelists and members of the public offered testimony, with medical representatives requesting protections for clinical and research operations [59:46], labor leaders discussing job creation [1:02:03], and environmental advocates raising concerns over public health and utility costs [1:06:40], [2:04:09]. No votes or formal decisions were taken before the hearing concluded [2:12:14].
